---
title: "Random slopes"
execute: {warning: false, message: false}
---

The [random-intercept model](random-intercepts.qmd) allows participant baselines to vary while holding the lexical-frequency association constant. A random-slope model also lets that association vary across participants. The [structured-data page](structured-data.qmd) identifies which predictors vary within each grouping unit, and the [correlated-predictors page](correlated-predictors.qmd) explains why a partial association still depends on available predictor combinations.

The [random-effect framework](fixed-and-random-effects.qmd) treats participant-specific slopes as deviations from a population slope. Their [standard deviations and covariances](../random-variables-and-distributions/variance-and-covariance.qmd) describe variation and co-variation across the fitted participant population. A varying lexical-frequency association is supported by repeated MALD trials; it should not be promoted to a stable participant phenotype beyond this task.

A participant-specific slope is supported only when participants contribute within-person predictor contrasts. The MALD incidence table supplies that check before the added covariance is derived and fitted.

## Adding a participant-specific association

For MALD trial $i$, participant $p$, and word $w$, write

$$
Y_{pwi}
=\beta_0+b_{0p}
+(\beta_f+b_{1p})x_{wi}^{(f)}
+\beta_d x_{wi}^{(d)}
+\beta_t x_{pwi}^{(t)}
+c_w+\varepsilon_{pwi}.
$$

The population frequency association is $\beta_f$. Participant $p$ has association

$$
\beta_f+b_{1p}.
$$

The intercept and slope deviations are modeled jointly:

$$
\begin{pmatrix}b_{0p}\\b_{1p}\end{pmatrix}
\sim
\mathcal N
\left(
\begin{pmatrix}0\\0\end{pmatrix},
\boldsymbol\Sigma_p
\right).
$$

The frequency-slope standard deviation describes how much the fitted lexical-frequency association varies across the participant population.

## Checking that the design contains the contrast

A participant-specific frequency association requires frequency variation within participants. A word has one lexical frequency, so repeated responses to that word cannot identify an item-specific frequency slope.

```{r}
#| label: mald-random-slopes
library(lme4)
library(ggplot2)

mald <- read.csv("data/mald/mald-connected-trials.csv")
mald <- subset(mald, correct == 1L)

standardize <- function(x) {
  as.numeric(scale(x))
}

mald$z_frequency <- standardize(mald$log_frequency_subtlex)
mald$z_duration <- standardize(mald$log_duration)
mald$z_trial <- standardize(mald$trial_order)

within_participant_range <- aggregate(
  z_frequency ~ participant_id,
  data = mald,
  FUN = function(x) diff(range(x))
)
within_item_range <- aggregate(
  z_frequency ~ item,
  data = mald,
  FUN = function(x) diff(range(x))
)

fit <- lmer(
  log_rt ~ z_frequency + z_duration + z_trial +
    (1 + z_frequency | participant_id) +
    (1 | item),
  data = mald,
  control = lmerControl(
    optimizer = "bobyqa",
    optCtrl = list(maxfun = 200000L)
  )
)

support_summary <- c(
  minimum_participant_range = min(within_participant_range$z_frequency),
  maximum_participant_range = max(within_participant_range$z_frequency),
  maximum_item_range = max(within_item_range$z_frequency)
)
support_summary
```

Every participant spans a nonzero range of standardized frequency, whereas the maximum within-item range is `r sprintf("%.1f", max(within_item_range$z_frequency))`. The data thus support participant frequency slopes but not word-specific frequency slopes.

Two actual participants make the support requirement concrete:

```{r}
#| label: two-participant-frequency-ranges
#| echo: true
range_examples <- within_participant_range[
  order(within_participant_range$z_frequency)[c(1L, nrow(within_participant_range))],
]
range_examples
```

Both have nonzero within-listener contrasts, though their ranges differ. By contrast, every repetition of a given word carries the same lexical-frequency value, so an item-specific frequency slope would ask the data to identify a within-item contrast that does not exist.

## Comparing raw and fitted participant relations

We display six participants selected across the fitted slope distribution. Points are within-participant raw bin means. Lines include participant intercept and frequency-slope deviations, set duration and trial order to their standardized means, and set the word effect to zero.

```{r}
#| label: plot-mald-slopes
participant_effects <- ranef(fit)$participant_id
participant_slopes <- data.frame(
  participant_id = rownames(participant_effects),
  slope_deviation = participant_effects[["z_frequency"]],
  row.names = NULL
)
participant_slopes <- participant_slopes[
  order(participant_slopes$slope_deviation),
]

selected_index <- unique(round(seq(
  1,
  nrow(participant_slopes),
  length.out = 6L
)))
selected_participants <- participant_slopes$participant_id[selected_index]

selected_raw <- mald[
  mald$participant_id %in% selected_participants,
]
selected_raw$participant_id <- factor(
  selected_raw$participant_id,
  levels = selected_participants
)
selected_raw$frequency_bin <- ave(
  selected_raw$z_frequency,
  selected_raw$participant_id,
  FUN = function(x) {
    cut(
      x,
      breaks = unique(quantile(x, seq(0, 1, length.out = 7L))),
      include.lowest = TRUE,
      labels = FALSE
    )
  }
)
selected_bins <- aggregate(
  cbind(z_frequency, log_rt) ~ participant_id + frequency_bin,
  data = selected_raw,
  FUN = mean
)

participant_grid <- expand.grid(
  participant_id = factor(
    selected_participants,
    levels = selected_participants
  ),
  z_frequency = seq(-2, 2, length.out = 80L),
  z_duration = 0,
  z_trial = 0
)
participant_grid$item <- factor(
  levels(factor(mald$item))[[1L]],
  levels = levels(factor(mald$item))
)
participant_grid$fitted_log_rt <- predict(
  fit,
  newdata = participant_grid,
  re.form = ~(1 + z_frequency | participant_id),
  allow.new.levels = TRUE
)

ggplot(selected_bins, aes(x = z_frequency, y = log_rt)) +
  geom_point(color = "grey45", size = 1.2) +
  geom_line(
    data = participant_grid,
    aes(y = fitted_log_rt),
    color = "#1F5A85",
    linewidth = 0.7
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~participant_id, ncol = 3) +
  labs(
    x = "SUBTLEX log frequency (standardized)",
    y = "Log response time"
  ) +
  theme_classic()
```

## How the dependence changes

Two trials from participant $p$ share $b_{0p}$, and their covariance also contains the slope contribution

$$
x_{pwi}^{(f)}x_{pwi'}^{(f)}\tau_1^2
$$

plus intercept-slope covariance terms when the deviations are correlated. Writing $\tau_{01}=\operatorname{Cov}(b_{0p},b_{1p})$, the full participant contribution is

$$
\operatorname{Cov}(Y_{pi},Y_{pi'})
=\tau_0^2+(x_i^{(f)}+x_{i'}^{(f)})\tau_{01}
+x_i^{(f)}x_{i'}^{(f)}\tau_1^2.
$$

Trial pairs at different frequency values thus need not have the same covariance. A constant participant ICC no longer summarizes every pair.

The model still imposes one population frequency coefficient. The random slope states that this average is incomplete as a description of individual listeners. Its inclusion is licensed by both the within-participant frequency range and the goal of generalizing the frequency association across listeners.

## Recap and check

1. Is a random slope the same as a fixed interaction with participant labels? No. Separate fixed interactions do not impose a shared population distribution or partial pooling.
2. Why is no item frequency slope fit? Frequency has zero within-item variation, so that slope is unidentified from repeated responses to the same word.

The [next page](random-effect-correlations.qmd) examines the covariance between participant baselines and these frequency slopes.
